whyItExists.short: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) fills the gaps when HTML semantics alone cannot describe complex UI patterns to assistive technologies.
whyItExists.problem: A custom dropdown, a live search result list, or a tab panel has no native HTML equivalent. Screen readers see a div — they have no idea it's a menu.
whyItExists.solution: ARIA attributes (role, aria-label, aria-expanded, aria-hidden, aria-live…) overlay semantic meaning onto any element so screen readers can announce it correctly.
whyItExists.impact: Over 1 billion people worldwide have a disability. ARIA makes complex web apps accessible to users of screen readers, switch devices, and braille displays.

explainModes.beginner: ARIA is extra information you add to HTML so screen readers understand what elements do. aria-label gives something a spoken name. aria-hidden hides things from screen readers. role tells a screen reader what type of thing an element is.
explainModes.simple: ARIA attributes extend HTML's accessibility. role overrides or adds a semantic role. aria-label provides a spoken label. aria-expanded tells screen readers if something is open or closed. aria-hidden removes elements from the accessibility tree.
explainModes.standard: The first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA if native HTML semantics work. Use button not div role=button. Add ARIA only when building custom components with no semantic HTML equivalent. aria-label/aria-labelledby name elements; aria-describedby adds descriptions; aria-expanded/aria-selected/aria-checked communicate state.
explainModes.technical: ARIA attributes modify the accessibility tree — a parallel structure browsers expose to assistive tech. role sets the semantic type. aria-label overrides the accessible name computation. aria-live regions (polite/assertive) announce dynamic content changes without focus movement. aria-controls, aria-owns, and aria-haspopup communicate relationships between elements.
explainModes.deepDive: The accessible name computation algorithm (AccName) follows a priority order: aria-labelledby > aria-label > native label > title. aria-labelledby can reference multiple element IDs, concatenating their text. aria-live=polite queues announcements; assertive interrupts immediately (use sparingly). The aria-atomic attribute controls whether live regions announce partial or full updates. ARIA 1.2 adds new roles like log, timer, and status for common dynamic patterns.

content.text: **The first rule of ARIA: use native HTML first.** A `<button>` is always better than `<div role="button">` — it gets keyboard focus and click handling for free.
Use ARIA when you build custom components that have no HTML equivalent.
**aria-label** gives an element an accessible name — what the screen reader announces:

content.label: aria-label examples
content.code:
<!-- Icon button with no visible text -->
<button aria-label="Close dialog">
  <svg>...</svg>
</button>

<!-- Two navs on the same page -->
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">...</nav>
<nav aria-label="Footer navigation">...</nav>

<!-- Search input -->
<input type="search" aria-label="Search lessons">

content.title: Test with a real screen reader
content.body: Windows: NVDA (free) + Chrome. Mac: VoiceOver (built-in, Cmd+F5) + Safari. Mobile: TalkBack (Android) or VoiceOver (iOS). Reading ARIA docs is not a substitute for testing.

content.question: What is the first rule of ARIA?
options: Always add ARIA to every element
Use native HTML semantics before ARIA
content.explanation: The W3C's first rule of ARIA is: if you can use a native HTML element with the semantics already built in, use it. ARIA fills gaps — it doesn't replace native HTML.

content.question: What does aria-hidden="true" do?
options: Removes the element from the DOM
Hides the element from screen readers only
content.explanation: aria-hidden removes an element from the accessibility tree — screen readers skip it. The element remains fully visible and interactive for sighted users. Use it for decorative icons and visual noise.

faq.q: When should I use aria-label vs aria-labelledby?
faq.a: Prefer aria-labelledby when there is already visible text on the page that serves as the label — it references that text so there is no duplication. Use aria-label when there is no visible label text (icon-only buttons, for example).

faq.q: Can I add ARIA to any element?
faq.a: Technically yes, but some role+element combinations are invalid (like role=button on an input). Follow the ARIA in HTML spec which lists allowed role+element combinations.

faq.q: Is ARIA required for every website?
faq.a: No. A website built with correct semantic HTML (headings, landmarks, labels, buttons, links) is largely accessible without any ARIA. ARIA is needed for complex interactive components: carousels, modals, custom dropdowns, tabs, and live regions.

examples: GitHub's command palette uses role=dialog, aria-label, and aria-live for search results
Twitter uses aria-expanded on the 'Show more' tweet thread toggle
